notes.urn:cts:greekLit:tlg0081.tlg001.perseus-: θεοῦ χθονίου in the inscription may mean 'native god' or 'god of the underworld'.
Line 3: the Greek has Kelerios for the man usually called Celer.
Dionysius calls lupa a Greek word, as the text says.
The text places the rite 'a little after the spring equinox, in the month of May', as given.
καλαῦροψ is properly a herdsman's staff; here it seems to mean the club.
Ῥῶμος, elsewhere rendered Remus, is given as Romus here, where he is Aeneas' son.
ὑπερπύροις ἀπαρχαῖς, rendered 'burnt first-fruits', is uncertain in sense.

nodes.text: Not long afterwards another Greek expedition put in to these parts of Italy, about the sixtieth year before the Trojan War, as the Romans themselves say, having set out from Pallantium, a city of Arcadia. The colony was led by Evander, said to be [the son] of Hermes and of a nymph native to the Arcadians, whom the Greeks say was Themis and represent as divinely inspired, while those who have written the Roman antiquities call her in their native tongue Carmenta; in the Greek language the nymph's name would be *Thespiōdos* [oracle-singer]; for the Romans call songs *carmina*, and they agree that this woman, being possessed by a divine spirit, used to foretell in song to the people what was going to happen.

This expedition was not sent out by common resolution; rather, when the people fell into faction, the defeated party withdrew of its own accord. At that time it happened that Faunus had succeeded to the kingship of the Aborigines, a descendant of Ares, as they say, a man both energetic and shrewd, whom the Romans honour as one of their local divinities with sacrifices and songs. This man received the Arcadians, who were few, with great friendliness, and gave them as much of his own land as they wanted.

I know of none of these things being done [for him]. The Arcadians, then, having settled together beneath the hill, ordered their settlement in other respects according to the customs of their homeland, and set up shrines, first to Lycaean Pan at the direction of Themis (for to the Arcadians Pan is the most ancient and most honoured of the gods), having found a suitable spot, which the Romans call the Lupercal, but we would call the Lycaeum.

A few years after the Arcadians another Greek expedition arrived in Italy, led by Heracles, who had come after subduing Iberia and all the lands as far as the setting of the sun. Some of his followers asked Heracles to be released from the campaign, stayed behind in these parts and founded a settlement, having found a suitable hill about three stades distant from Pallantium, which is now called the Capitoline, but by the people of that time was called the Saturnian, as one might say in Greek the Cronian.

There is also another story told as myth by the inhabitants, that before the reign of Zeus, Cronus held power in this land, and that the life said [to have been lived] in his time, abundant in everything the seasons bring forth, was found among no others more than among themselves.

This the Romans still continued to do even down to my time, a little after the spring equinox, in the month of May, on the so-called Ides, which they mean to be the middle day of the month; on this day, after first offering the sacrifices prescribed by law, the so-called pontiffs, the most eminent of the priests, and with them the virgins who guard the undying fire, and the praetors, and those of the other citizens for whom it is lawful to attend the rites, throw from the sacred bridge into the stream of the Tiber images made in the likeness of men, thirty in number, Argei

of them became the accuser of the theft. So Cacus, when his crime had been exposed, turned to resistance and called on those who used to camp in the fields with him; but Heracles beat him to death with his club, and having driven out the cattle, since he saw that the place was well suited for harbouring evildoers, he pulled the cave down on top of him with his staff. Having cleansed himself of the killing in the river, he set up near the spot an altar of Zeus Heuresios [the Finder], which is in Rome beside the Trigemina Gate, and sacrificed a calf to the god as a thank-offering for the finding of the cattle. This sacrifice the city of the Romans was still performing in my time, observing in it all the Greek customs, just as he established them.

Among those overcome in battle, they say, was also Cacus, of whom the Romans tell a myth, a chieftain utterly barbarous and ruler of savage men, who became his enemy; he occupied strongholds and was therefore a trouble to his neighbours. When he learned that Heracles had encamped in the plain nearby, he equipped himself like a brigand and made a sudden raid while the army was asleep, and as much of the booty as he came upon unguarded

For the Rutulians marched against him in full force from their cities, and with them Mezentius, king of the Tyrrhenians, fearing for his own land; for he was vexed to see the Greek power already growing great. A fierce battle took place not far from Lavinium, and many fell on both sides; when night came on the armies separated, and since the body of Aeneas was nowhere to be seen, some conjectured that he had passed over to the gods, others that he had perished in the river beside which the battle was fought.

And the Latins build him a hero-shrine adorned with an inscription such as this: “Of the father, the god of the land, who governs the stream of the river Numicius.” But there are some who say it was built by Aeneas for Anchises, who had died a year before this war. It is a mound, not large, and around it are trees planted in rows, worth seeing.

But since there is much dispute both about the time of the founding and about the founders of the city, I too did not think I should pass over it cursorily as though everyone agreed on it. For Cephalon of Gergis, a very ancient writer, says that the city was founded in the second generation after the Trojan War by those who had escaped from Ilium with Aeneas, and he declares its founder to be Romus, the leader of the colony, and that this man was one of the sons of Aeneas; he says that Aeneas had four sons, Ascanius, Euryleon, Romulus and Romus. Demagoras too and Agathyllus and many others give the same date and the same leader of the colony.

In the fourth year after, Ilia went to a sacred grove of Ares to fetch pure water to be used for the sacrifices, and someone ravished her in the precinct. Some declare that he was one of the maiden's suitors, in love with the girl; others, that it was Amulius himself, acting not so much from desire as from design, armed in such a way that he would appear most terrifying, and making his appearance as hard to recognise as he could;

Numitor's herds, which he managed; and they say that the one who nursed the children and gave them the breast was not a she-wolf but, as is likely, a woman named Laurentia who lived with Faustulus, to whom, since she had once made a public trade of her body's bloom, the people living around Pallantium gave the nickname Lupa; this is a Greek and ancient [term] applied to women who hire out the pleasures of love, who are now called by a more decent name *hetairai* [companions]. And some who did not know this invented the myth of the she-wolf, since in the language which the Latin people speak this animal is called *lupa*. When the children had been weaned from milk, they were given by those rearing them to Gabii, a city lying not far from

In this battle, some say, Faustulus, who had brought up the youths, wishing to end the brothers' strife and able to achieve nothing, threw himself unarmed into the midst of the combatants, eager to meet the swiftest death, and that is what happened. Some say too that the stone lion which stood in the chief place of the Roman Forum, beside the Rostra, was set over the body of Faustulus, who was buried where he fell by those who found him.

When Remus had died in the battle, Romulus, having won a most pitiable victory over his brother and through the citizens' slaughter of one another, buried Remus in Remoria, since while alive too he had clung to that place for the founding; and he himself, giving way to grief and remorse for what had been done, sank into despair of life. But when Laurentia, who had taken them in as newborns and reared them and loved them no less than a mother, entreated and comforted him, he was persuaded by her and rose up; and gathering the Latins, as many as had not been killed in the battle, a little more than three thousand out of the very large number there had been at first, when he was sending out the colony,

he founded Pallantium. This, then, seems to me the most credible of the accounts of the death of Remus. Yet let it be told also if any other version has been handed down. Some say, then, that he yielded the leadership to Romulus, but, vexed and angry at the deceit, when the wall had been built, wishing to show that the fortification was feeble, he said, “But this, at any rate, any enemy of yours could get over without trouble, as I do,” and at once leapt over it; and that Celer, one of those standing on the wall, who was overseer of the works, said, “But this enemy, at any rate, any of us could ward off without trouble,” and struck him on the head with his spade and killed him on the spot. Such, then, is said to have been the end of the brothers' quarrel.

But the myths handed down about them, in which there are blasphemies or slanders against them, he judged to be wicked, useless and indecent, and unworthy not only of gods but even of good men, and he rejected them all, and prepared people to speak and to think the best about the gods, attributing to them no conduct unworthy of their blessed nature.

For among the Romans it is not said that Uranus was castrated by his own sons, nor that Cronus did away with his own offspring for fear of an attack from them, nor that Zeus overthrew the rule of Cronus and shut his own father up in the prison of Tartarus; nor indeed [are there] wars and wounds and

The festival then instituted by Romulus the Romans have continued to celebrate even down to my time, calling it the Consualia; at it an underground altar, set up beside the greatest of the hippodromes, is uncovered by digging away the earth around it and honoured with sacrifices and burnt first-fruits, and a race of horses, both yoked and unyoked, is held. The god to whom they perform these rites is called Consus by the Romans; some, translating [the name] into our language, say that he is Poseidon the Earth-shaker, and say that he has been honoured with an underground altar for this reason, that this god holds the earth.

which stands a little above the forum. They also founded shrines and consecrated altars to the gods to whom they had made vows during the battles: Romulus to Zeus Orthosios [the Upholder] beside the so-called Mugonian Gate, which leads from the Sacred Way to the Palatine, because the god, hearing his prayers, had made his army stop its flight and turn to resist; and Tatius to the Sun and the Moon, to Cronus and Rhea, and besides these to Hestia and Hephaestus, Artemis and Enyalius, and other gods whose names are hard to render in the Greek language; and in all the curiae he set up tables to Hera, called Curitis, which stand even to this day.

Those who make the story about him more mythical say that while he was holding an assembly in the camp, darkness swept down out of a clear sky and a great storm burst, and he vanished; and they have believed that the man was carried off by his father Ares;

but those who write the more credible version say that he died at the hands of his own citizens. As the cause of his killing they allege the release, without common consent and contrary to custom, of the hostages he had taken from the Veientes; and that he no longer behaved in the same way towards the oldest citizens and those enrolled later, but held the former in greater honour and slighted the newcomers; and his cruelty and arrogance in punishing wrongdoers (for he had ordered some Romans accused of brigandage against their neighbours, men neither obscure nor few, to be thrown down the cliff, having judged the case alone by himself); but most of all that he already seemed harsh and arrogant, and to be conducting his rule no longer like a king but more like a tyrant.

But those who strip everything mythical from history say that the story about Egeria was invented by Numa, so that those who feared the divine might more readily pay heed to him and gladly accept the laws he laid down as coming from the gods.

A woman who was not a native came to the tyrant wishing to sell nine books full of Sibylline oracles. When Tarquin refused to buy the books at the price asked, she went away and burned three of them; and not long afterwards she brought the remaining six and offered them at the same price.
